Voltaire. A French Enlightenment writer, philosopher, and polemicist from sixteen ninety-four to seventeen seventy-eight whose wit, prolific output, and combative advocacy for reason, tolerance, and individual liberty made him the intellectual voice of the eighteenth century. Through satire, history, philosophy, and correspondence with royalty and fellow thinkers, he attacked superstition, religious dogmatism, and tyranny, establishing the template for the modern public intellectual.

Born François-Marie Arouet into a middle-class family, he adopted the pen name Voltaire, which became synonymous with Enlightenment ideals and the power of satire as a weapon against authority. He was imprisoned in the Bastille twice for his writings and political affiliations. Yet he was exiled from France multiple times and continued publishing under pseudonyms and through clandestine networks, making suppression of his work impossible.

Candide, his novella-length masterpiece of satire published in seventeen fifty-nine, mocks the philosophy of his day—especially Leibniz's claim that all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds. He chronicles a naive young man's brutal education through suffering and absurdity. The work became the paradigm of Enlightenment satire.

Voltaire was prolific across genres. He wrote over fifty plays, historical works, philosophical essays, and thousands of letters. His correspondence was itself a medium of Enlightenment thought, connecting European intellectuals across borders. He advocated relentlessly for the separation of church and state, religious toleration, freedom of conscience, and legal reform. His campaigns contributed to real-world changes, including interventions in cases of judicial injustice.

He cultivated relationships with power. He corresponded with Frederick the Second of Prussia and Catherine the Great of Russia and French nobility, using access to influence policy toward Enlightenment goals. He championed reason and empirical observation against superstition and revealed religious dogma. His attacks on religious fanaticism, captured in the phrase "Écrasez l'infâme!"—crush the infamy—defined the Enlightenment's combat against clerical authority.

Voltaire embodied the philosophical movement of the Enlightenment and shaped it. He gave the Enlightenment its voice, wit, and moral urgency. The French Revolution that followed his death drew directly on his writings on liberty, reason, and the critique of tyranny and privilege. He advocated for Shakespeare in France, translating and defending him against French classical orthodoxy, helping establish the Bard as a universal figure. He stood at the philosophical intersection of empiricism and reason, defending systematic thought against superstition. His essays like the Philosophical Dictionary and countless treatises made philosophy accessible and combative, not merely academic.
